subtitle: "Ideas you may already recognise"

This first refresher begins with the version of topology many people have
already encountered: the coffee cup and doughnut. Its purpose is to recover
useful intuition, connect that intuition to data, and identify where the
metaphor stops being sufficient.

You can follow the main course after reading this page. The separate
[Topology refresher B](topology-survival-guide.qmd) supplies open sets,
topological spaces, metric details and finer distinctions when you want the
formal background.

## The familiar example

A solid coffee cup with one handle and a solid doughnut each have one tunnel.
In the rubber-sheet metaphor, one can be continuously reshaped into the other
without cutting, gluing or tearing. A suitable deformation narrows the cup,
thickens its handle and rounds the result into a torus.

This reversible continuous correspondence is called a **homeomorphism**. Two
spaces related this way are **homeomorphic**. Topology deliberately ignores
their different lengths, angles, curvature and coordinates while retaining
their continuous organisation.

![A coffee cup and a torus are connected by a reversible deformation when both are treated as solid surfaces with one handle or tunnel.](../../assets/topology-cup-torus.svg){fig-alt="A schematic coffee cup with one handle is connected by a reversible deformation arrow to a torus."}

::: {.qualification}
**† Qualification.** The material description matters. A hollow vessel, its
thin surface and a completely solid object are different spaces. The standard
metaphor assumes objects chosen so that the handle and torus represent the
same one-tunnel organisation.
:::

## What topology keeps and forgets

Geometry asks about distance, angle, curvature, coordinates and scale.
Topology asks which relationships survive reversible continuous deformation.
For elementary examples this includes:

- how many connected pieces there are;
- whether paths can move between regions;
- whether loop-like or void-like structure is present; and
- whether deformation can remove a feature without cutting or filling.

Neither lens replaces the other. A circle and a highly stretched ellipse have
the same topology but different geometry. A filled disc and its circular
outline may occupy the same outer location, but only the outline supports a
non-filled loop.

## Homeomorphism, homotopy and homology

These terms answer different questions.

| Idea | High-level question | What it provides |
|---|---|---|
| Homeomorphism | Are the spaces the same up to reversible continuous deformation? | A strong equivalence of spaces |
| Homotopy equivalence | Do they have the same broad continuous shape after contractible detail is ignored? | A weaker equivalence |
| Homology | How many independent cycle-like features occur in each dimension? | Algebraic invariants, not a complete description |

A filled triangle and a single point are not homeomorphic, but the triangle
can contract to a point and is homotopy equivalent to it. An outline triangle
cannot contract to a point while remaining inside the outline. Homology sees
that distinction through a nonzero $H_1$ class for the outline.

Homology is deliberately incomplete. Different spaces can have the same
homology. That makes it a computable summary, not a universal definition of
shape.

::: {.callout-note title="Expert-level detail: safe to skip"}
Precise constructions of homotopies, induced maps and counterexamples where
homology fails to distinguish spaces belong to algebraic topology. The main
course needs only the hierarchy above: homeomorphism is stronger than homotopy
equivalence, and homology is an invariant that may agree even when the spaces
are not equivalent.
:::

## Why this is not yet topology for data

A scatter plot is a finite set of observations, not a rubber sheet. Two
finite samples are not automatically homeomorphic to the continuous objects
they appear to trace. In fact, with sufficiently small neighbourhoods, every
point of a finite point cloud can be isolated.

TDA therefore inserts a construction:

$$
\text{observations}
\longrightarrow
\text{neighbourhood representation}
\longrightarrow
\text{homology}.
$$

A metric or relation decides which observations count as near. A graph,
simplicial complex or cubical complex records those relationships. Homology is
then computed on that constructed representation. Persistent homology repeats
the calculation across a range of thresholds.

::: {.data-translation}
**Data-analysis translation.** Standardising variables, selecting a metric,
constructing an embedding and choosing a neighbourhood scale change which
records become neighbours. The topological output describes the data through
those choices, not independently of them.
:::

::: {.applied-translation}
**Dynamical systems translation.** A continuous attractor may be observed only
through finitely sampled states. A point-cloud complex can test which
connected or recurrent organisation the samples support across resolution.
It does not automatically prove that the complex has recovered the invariant
set or its mechanism.
:::

## What to retain

You are ready for Week 1 if you can explain that:

1. topology deliberately forgets metric detail;
2. the coffee cup and doughnut illustrate reversible continuous deformation;
3. homeomorphism, homotopy and homology are not synonyms;
4. finite data require a representation before homology is computed; and
5. the result belongs first to that representation.

Continue to [Week 1](index.qmd). Use [Topology refresher B](topology-survival-guide.qmd)
when the course needs precise language about sets, metrics, open sets,
continuity or topological spaces.
